attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post; not a quote of anyone else.

semantics.note: Faithful present-tense comparison of facility classes. 'Things like' social media or streaming is kept as the comparator. The range is preserved.

contract.note: The plain reading is fair and ordinary: a general facility-level power-capacity comparison, as his own MW examples suggest. It rightly bars cherry-picked extremes and keeps announced and operating capacity separate.

evidence.note: IEA illustrative 25 MW conventional vs 100 MW hyperscale (about 4x), from April 2025. This is an earlier period and generic conventional-vs-hyperscale, not a representative comparison with social-media or streaming sites.
IREN's 50 MW GPU site as of Dec 2025. One smaller AI-related facility with no matched social-media or streaming comparator. It cannot settle the general ratio.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no representative, matched data on AI facilities vs social-media or streaming facilities around August 2026. The IEA 4x illustration is from an earlier period and a different comparator class. The 50 MW IREN site is a single example. Neither confirms nor refutes a typical 10–100x range.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence in his own post.

semantics.note: 'Guaranteed to change' is a firm forecast with no deadline. The paraphrase softens 'whatever you're paying' and 'guaranteed' a little, but keeps the commitment and the stated reason.

contract.note: Reading the claim as about price or plan terms is ordinary. Context also treats less value at the same price as a change, which the contract notes. Requiring broad change across vendors fits 'whatever you're paying'. The early-resolution rule of three vendors is reasonable.

evidence.note: Kingy index, Oct 2026: no list-price changes among continuing items, and median subscription prices unchanged. With no deadline, no change two months in is not failure, so this is context rather than contradiction.
Google announced a doubling of one API price, effective Dec 1, 2026, after the evaluation date. It is one vendor and a future change, so it does not meet the early-resolution rule.

New Gemini Code Assist subscriptions withdrawn Oct 9, 2026. One product from one vendor, with no cost reason given, so it is not the broad list-price change across three vendors the contract requires.

reviews.rationale: No deadline was stated, and the early-resolution rule (list-price changes for main paid plans at three or more leading vendors, with cost reasons) is not met by the cutoff. The evidence shows one announced Google API change and one product withdrawal. Unchanged medians do not refute an open-ended forecast.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Keeps 'guaranteed', 'at some point', the three-way disjunction, and the link to shifting economics. It is a firm forecast with no deadline.

contract.note: Reading the generic second-person 'you' as typical paying users of a major service, with any one disjunct sufficing, is an ordinary reading. Full universality could never be shown. The cost link rests on reported framing, which the contract allows.

evidence.note: ITdaily, Aug 31, 2026: from Sept 14, paid Claude users lose 17% of current weekly Claude Code limits. This is a rate-limit shift after the post.
MindStudio confirms the change covers Pro, Max, Team and Enterprise, replacing a temporary boost. It took effect Sept 14, before the evaluation date.
The reporter ties Anthropic's limit management to rising costs, which supplies the reported economic link the rule needs. This is the reporter's framing, not Anthropic's stated reason.
The cut ended a temporary promotion, and session limits stayed doubled. This narrows how severe the change was, but it is still a shift in rate limits for paying users.

reviews.rationale: After the Aug 25 post, Anthropic changed weekly Claude Code limits across all paid plans from Sept 14, a 17% cut from current levels. Reporting ties limit management to costs. This meets the early-resolution rule. The claim is a weak disjunction with no deadline, so one service's change shows the outcome happened, not that it was guaranteed for every user.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: The 'objective disaster' judgment is properly set aside. The factual core is cumulative capex above $260B and annual revenue outside OpenAI below $11B. 'AI business' matches the context.

contract.note: Using realized FY2026 revenue is an ordinary reading of 'annual revenue'. The contract rightly refuses to invent a capex start date or assume all capex served AI. The outcome depends on those unspecified choices.

evidence.note: Microsoft's Q3 FY26 disclosure of AI ARR above $37B. This is a run rate that includes OpenAI, not realized revenue excluding OpenAI. It is a company disclosure.
One quarter of company-wide capex ($41B, including leases) serving AI and non-AI workloads. It does not establish the cumulative AI-specific total.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no realized FY2026 AI revenue figure excluding OpenAI, and no reconciled cumulative AI capex with a defined start period. The run-rate figure and a single quarter's capex settle neither threshold.
